extracted.intended_audience: cartographers, topographers, engineers, geologists, and educated readers interested in map-making and map evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and describing the qualities required of a geographical/topographical map (accuracy, usefulness, artistic treatment, survey methods, and suggested bathymetric completeness), illustrated by a review of a Lake Tahoe map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness / primary mission
rubrics_metrics.description: So much for its usefulness, which is the first and principal mission of a map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good map must serve practical users (engineer, geologist, tourist, soldier, emigrant) — e.g., the map of Lake Tahoe should guide engineers in projects, geologists in studies, tourists on travels, soldiers on marches, and emigrants in search of a home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / minimal error
rubrics_metrics.description: In the end we have a map of which the error is, in general, inappreciable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy comes from combining reliable sources (reconnaissance, mountain sketches, barometrical heights on a precise geodetic basis, and incorporation of land-surveys) so that positional and topographic error is negligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost in time and money is comparatively insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The described American methods (rapid reconnaissance + mountain sketch + barometric height + geodetic basis + incorporation of other reliable information) produce accurate maps without large expenditure of time or money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic quality / graphic delineation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a work of art, graphically delineating the configuration of a district of surpassing beauty and variety of scenery, it will, perhaps, possess greater interest to the ordinary observer than any scientific value of accuracy and completeness could give it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A map's artistic effect (composition, shading, presentation of scenery variety) can increase public interest; the map should group specimens of all types of topographical form and use conventional signs effectively to produce an appealing graphic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic portrayal / fidelity to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The agricultural district ... the sharp and ragged peaks ... are all given true to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism is achieved by field observation (the draughtsman visiting the ground, making sketches from summits and advantageous points) and using those sketches to restore a natural effect to construction plots of contour-lines received from surveyors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field verification by draughtsman
rubrics_metrics.description: He visited the ground in person, and, from the summits of lofty peaks and other advantageous points, accumulated a series of sketches with the aid of which to restore a natural effect to the construction-plots of contour-lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal observation by the draughtsman (not merely relying on secondary survey data) preserves characteristic traits of form and surface that are hard to transmit between hands; this contributes to realistic and effective mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of rendering: hachures vs contours
rubrics_metrics.description: The map is finished in hachures, a method which is more intelligible to the unprofessional eye than that of contours, and which, in this case, is made especially effective by a free and artistic handling of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the method of relief representation appropriate to the audience and subject: hachures may be preferable for popular maps because they are more immediately intelligible; contours may be more technical. The rendering method must be executed with skill and appropriate artistic freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive slavishness to conventional schools
rubrics_metrics.description: The draughtsman who adheres too closely and conscientiously to Lehmann's or any other conventional diapason of shades is likely to construct a map whose geographical features are stiff, unnatural, and almost mechanical in their geometrical regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While conventions and standards are useful, excessive literal adherence can produce cold, inflexible maps; felicitous touches and extra shading that depart from rigid school rules can improve readability and aesthetic effect, especially for popular use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance man-made features with natural attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: This has an advantage over the maps of the thickly settled European countries, upon which the utilitarian features of roads, villages, and other works of man are so numerous as to obscure the natural attractions of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include human infrastructure where relevant, but avoid overloading the map with right angles and urban detail that detract from the landscape's beauty or the map's legibility; choose a balance appropriate to the map's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject suitability / comprehensiveness of topographical specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person were called upon to construct an ideal map which should group together specimens of all types of topographical form and the conventional signs known to the draughtsman, he could hardly derive from his imagination a chart more comprehensive than this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ideal subject for cartographical expression contains varied and instructive terrain; the map should present representative examples of topographical forms and conventional signs to maximize instructional and expressive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include bathymetric/soundings data where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: It is still incomplete, and it is to be hoped that provision may yet be made for a series of soundings with which to illustrate the very remarkable configuration of the bottom of the lake. ... the geographical map of the future, and especially the geological chart, will portray surfaces below as well as above water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps of lakes or seas should include submarine surfaces (soundings, bathymetric contours or faint/blue broken contour-lines) rather than decorative 'ripple-lines' which give no real idea of submarine configuration; this adds scientific and possibly economic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid decorative but misleading shoreline symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ripple-lines' with which shores are now sometimes represented ... give no idea of the additional character which a map would derive from a real plot of its surface below water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on purely decorative shore symbols if the intent is to inform about submarine topography; prefer real bathymetric plotting to concentric ripple patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combined surveying methods appropriate to large territories
rubrics_metrics.description: The methods in question combine the rapid reconnaissance, the mountain sketch, and the barometrical height upon a precise geodetic basis, incorporating all reliable information attainable from other sources, especially the land-surveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For extensive territories, adopt a hybrid survey approach (reconnaissance + sketches + barometric heights + geodetic control + integration of existing land-surveys) to achieve completeness and reliability efficiently.
